work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Foolishness is the mother of all vices.
‘God loves no one except the person who lives with wisdom’ (Wisdom 7:28).
The good of an unviolated and blameless nature.
translator_notes: The final fragment is a phrase Augustine quotes from Julian about human nature. The Virgil and Sirach material belongs to Augustine’s response.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Those who either neglected to learn what ought to be known, or are unafraid to condemn what they do not know.
In the noonday of discovered truth, without the shadow of ignorance, you rave through envy of me.
Envy immediately torments the very author from whom it arises.
One and the same vice cannot be both sin and punishment for sin.
translator_notes: The second excerpt’s pronouns are adapted from Augustine’s report. The final claim repeats the position previously recovered in Against Julian 5.9.36.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “After finishing your preface, in which you labored, as you usually do, to prove what I myself preach, ‘that God is the maker of human beings,’ you then set out my words, where I said: ‘A human being who is born of the desire of the flesh is born to the world, not to God; but he is born to God when he is reborn of water and the Spirit.’”

“You lie in wait for these words of mine so as to assert that it must be understood from them that I said that whatever belongs to the world belongs to the devil, because, of course, I had said elsewhere ‘that those who are born from the union of bodies belong to the devil’s jurisdiction,’ asserting, that is, that they ‘are rescued from the power of darkness when they are reborn in Christ.’”
translator_notes: The quotation about birth and rebirth is Augustine’s own Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.19.21, which Julian set out to refute; ‘God is the maker of human beings’ is the thesis of Julian’s preface. Augustine’s answer from John’s Gospel and letter is not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The grace of Christ’s mysteries is rich in many gifts.
Rather, he shows them to be his own by raising what he made in them through additional benefits, before their own obedient exercise of will.
translator_notes: Julian is describing baptismal benefits to infants. Augustine’s initial extracts from his own book and his Mark 16:16 objection are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Let us consider the point at issue in this chapter, where he says: ‘God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us’ (Romans 5:8). You want this to be thought said with infants excepted.”
“But you, already in your first book, crying out against us, said: ‘Christ died for infants too.’”
translator_notes: ‘Christ died for infants too’ is Julian’s wording, recalled from his first book. Augustine’s argument that Christ died only for those dead in sin is his answer and is not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “What I said in my book, which you oppose, is entirely true: ‘For that what was forgiven in the parent is passed on in the offspring happens in wonderful ways, but still it happens; and because the way itself is not traced out by easy reasoning, nor explained in speech, unbelievers do not believe it.’ You lay a false trap for these words of mine, as though I had said that it can ‘neither be grasped by reason nor explained in speech,’ taking away from it what I said, ‘not easy,’ whether of ‘reasoning’ or of ‘speech.’ ‘No’ reasoning, which is what you say, is one thing; ‘not easy’ reasoning, which is what I said, is another.”
translator_notes: The first quotation is from Augustine’s own book; Julian’s version of it, as Augustine reports, left out ‘not easy’. The disputed reading is kept as Augustine reports it.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Examples give no support to something that cannot be defended in itself.
translator_notes: Julian applies this to Augustine’s olive-tree analogy. Paul’s seed analogy is Augustine’s countertext, excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Albinus affirms that among all animals the crocodile alone moves its upper jaws; and fire, though destructive to everything else, is a plaything for the salamander.
Natural characteristics are not changed by an accidental occurrence.
A parent cannot transmit to offspring what the parent does not possess.
translator_notes: These ancient zoological claims are preserved as Julian’s cited examples, not endorsed as modern biology. Augustine repeats the last two definitions and supplies counterexamples; repetitions and counterexamples are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Curiosity usually wonders less at what it has understood. Against this, divine provision arranged that many things should arise from the earth, distinguished by countless properties.
translator_notes: Augustine also restates Julian’s point as the incomprehensibility of God’s works. Ecclesiastes 11:5 is Augustine’s supporting quotation, not explicitly Julian’s.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: By the nature of things, parents cannot be shown to hand on what they are believed to have lost. If they hand it on, they have not lost it.
translator_notes: Augustine compares this to an earlier Pelagian statement; that separate Pelagius quotation and Augustine’s circumcision exposition are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “See, the circumcised man hands on to the one born of him what he lacked in himself. What, then, is it that you say: ‘By the nature of things it cannot happen that people should be shown to hand on what they are believed to have lacked’? The foreskin is good, not evil, because God made it, just as you argued at great length about the wild olive.”

“So the circumcision of the flesh not only overturns, beyond doubt, that maxim of yours, general as it were, in which you say: ‘By the nature of things it cannot happen that a parent should hand on to his offspring what he himself lacked’ …”
translator_notes: Both quoted sentences are Julian’s maxim (also at 6.7.18), the second in the plural ‘you say’ for Julian and those who share his view. The wild olive was the subject of a long argument by Julian. Augustine’s explanation of circumcision as a sign is his answer and is not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: You tried to stir up the crowd against me.
Forgetting our single combat, you took refuge in the crowd.
With a treaty offered, it was agreed to settle the war, so that our contest would decide everyone’s battles.
translator_notes: The last excerpt contains an echo of Virgil, Aeneid 12.109, explicitly linked to Julian’s manner of speaking. Pronouns in the first two charges are adapted from Augustine’s report.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Do not mock the members of Christ with the name ‘sedentary craftsmen.’ … What is this: ‘When you begin to show them this, they will become more bitter toward me’? Do not lie to them, and they will not.”

“For I do not, as you falsely charge, ‘assert that they are the devil’s property,’ since I know they were redeemed by Christ’s blood; I do not ‘assign any marriages to the devil,’ insofar as they are marriages; I do not ‘make him out to be the craftsman of the genitals’; nor do I assert that he is ‘the arouser of men,’ except to unlawful acts, nor ‘the one who makes women fertile,’ nor ‘the maker of infants.’”
translator_notes: ‘Sedentary craftsmen’ is Julian’s scornful name for working people who sit at their trade. Who ‘you’ and ‘me’ are in the second quotation cannot be settled from the Latin; it is translated as printed. The list gives Julian’s charges, which Augustine denies; ‘except to unlawful acts’ is Augustine’s own qualification, though the transcription prints it inside the quotation.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Explain how sin can justly be charged to a person who neither wished nor was able to sin.
How can an act of choice be mixed into the condition of reproductive seed?
In what way did it happen?
translator_notes: Three separated questions. Augustine’s 2 Corinthians 5:14 response is excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Always busily working for his enemy’s profit.
translator_notes: Julian’s allegation about the God implied by Augustine’s teaching on infants, not Julian’s own description of God. Augustine repeats the allegation while disputing it.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The devil and God have made this agreement between them: God is to claim whatever is washed, and the devil whatever is born. But on this condition: God, by a power subject to another, is to make fruitful the very sexual union that the devil established.
translator_notes: A hostile characterization of Augustine’s position, which Augustine rejects. ‘Washed’ refers to baptism; Augustine expressly objects to Julian’s choice of this word instead of ‘reborn’ or ‘baptized.’

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “And yet we give thanks that you do not think this [that being washed is superfluous]. For you do not admit to the kingdom of God those who are born, unless they are washed; and so you show that being washed is far better than being born.”
translator_notes: ‘Washed’ is baptism. Augustine notes that Julian and those who share his view do not think it superfluous; the hypothetical argument before this and the Bible passages after it are Augustine’s own.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: No human sin can exist without an act of free choice.
One person is not held liable for another person’s sins.
translator_notes: Two claims from Julian’s list of matters the Christian faith does not doubt. Augustine’s qualifications and counterexamples are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: We must all appear before Christ’s judgment seat, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. (2 Corinthians 5:10)
translator_notes: The wording preserves the Latin biblical text Julian cites. Augustine’s questions about its application to infants and his other biblical citations are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Sexual desire is not wholly rebellious against the mind.
Let God be called the creator of infants who are such as befit God’s hands—that is, innocent infants.
translator_notes: Two separated statements; the phrase defining innocence is explicitly quoted as Julian’s addition.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Explain how the devil dares to claim as his own infants created in Christ—that is, in his power.
translator_notes: Julian’s demand is preserved within Augustine’s indirect quotation. Augustine’s reply about infants troubled by unclean spirits is excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: When God grants the glory of regeneration to infants who have deserved neither good nor evil by anything of their own, he teaches by that very act that they belong to his care, his right, and his dominion: he anticipates their will with the lavish gift of an inexpressible benefit.
translator_notes: Repeated argument: Augustine points back to Against Julian 3.3.8–9. The language about having deserved neither good nor evil recalls Romans 9:11; Augustine’s subsequent use of Romans 9:22–23 is his own.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Where the apostle says ‘by nature children of wrath,’ it can be understood as ‘truly children of wrath.’ (Ephesians 2:3)
translator_notes: Julian proposes a sense for ‘by nature’; Augustine argues against it from the established Latin translations. ‘Truly’ renders prorsus, with the force ‘altogether’ or ‘really.’

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “You run through the parts that make up the people (the multitude of Christians, which with good reason is most hostile to you), describing and mocking them one by one; among them you touch on ‘the students who attend lectures,’ and you say that they will shout against me: ‘O the times, O the morals!’ (Cicero, Against Catiline 1) And yet you dread the verdict of the crowd, where you could find supporters so loud for you that they would frighten me with Tullius’s words, because ‘I think that the genital part of the body comes from somewhere other than where the whole comes from.’”
translator_notes: ‘O the times, O the morals!’ is from Cicero’s first speech Against Catiline, used by Julian against Augustine. The charge about the genital part of the body is Julian’s, which Augustine denies. Augustine’s imagined reply and his further quotation from Cicero are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Even in a worn-out body, lust cannot be restrained.
translator_notes: Julian alleges that Augustine teaches this; Augustine explicitly denies it. The earlier ‘What times! What morals!’ repeats 6.11.34. The other quotation from Cicero and 1 Peter 3:9 belong to Augustine’s response.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “But which of us says: ‘This evil that infants draw from their origin can either exist, or has ever existed, without a substance in which it is’? As though we said it, you go looking for judges trained in logic, and you mock the common people.”
translator_notes: The sentence is Augustine’s formulation of the view Julian attacks; Augustine denies holding it. It is therefore presented as a reported accusation, not a verbatim statement of Julian’s own doctrine.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “And what sort of thing is it that, so as to persist in your perversity, you accuse Zosimus of blessed memory, bishop of the Apostolic See, of betraying his trust?”
translator_notes: No direct wording of Julian’s accusation is retained here. Augustine’s account of Zosimus, Innocent, and Caelestius is his rebuttal.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Julian excerpt in a reported argument
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Remember, indeed, how you insultingly throw up the dissension of the Roman people over the appointment of a bishop. I ask you whether those people did it by their own will. If you deny it, how do you defend free choice? But if you admit it, how do you call it ‘God’s vengeance’?”
translator_notes: Only ‘God’s vengeance’ is directly quoted. Augustine challenges Julian’s account of divine action and contrasts an earlier dispute involving Damasus and Ursicinus.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: You yourself have also changed your views: at the beginning of your conversion you held the same view that I do.
translator_notes: Augustine preserves this in indirect quotation and denies the claim. His ensuing autobiographical explanation and biblical references are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The baptized are only partly cleansed. This is more clearly apparent from your own words.
Grace does not make a person completely new.
translator_notes: Julian attributes these positions to Augustine; Augustine denies them. Julian had quoted Augustine’s On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.17.19–1.18.20, including Luke 20:34, 2 Corinthians 4:16, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and Romans 8:23. That long Augustine passage is not a surviving work of Julian and is identified here rather than reproduced as his prose.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The flesh is said to desire because the soul desires in a fleshly way.
The baptized person has nothing left to put to death.
translator_notes: The first statement explains Galatians 5:17. The second is a short quoted claim within Augustine’s objection from Colossians 3:5. Augustine’s other biblical quotations and his account of the eunuch Calligonus are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “You want it to seem so incredible ‘that in the womb of a baptized woman, whose body is the temple of God, a human being is formed who will be under the devil unless he is reborn to God from God.’”
translator_notes: The disputed claim is framed by Augustine as Julian’s objection to his theology. God’s temple recalls 1 Corinthians 6:19; birth from God recalls John 1:13. Augustine’s lengthy response is excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Julian allegations and an authority he invokes
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Where, then, did you hear or read me saying ‘that people are not renewed through baptism, but as if renewed; not freed, but as if freed; not saved, but as if saved’?”

“It is not I, then, who make God’s grace empty; but you, its enemy, seem to have gone after empty display, so as to bring into your argument Epicurus, who denied that the gods have a body, but something like a body, nor blood, but something like blood …”
“But which of us says ‘that whatever is done in the present age is to be blamed’?”
translator_notes: The first and last quotations give Julian’s account of Augustine’s teaching, which Augustine denies. ‘As if’ is repeated in the Latin, matching Epicurus’ ‘something like a body’. The Epicurean comparison goes back to Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods. Augustine’s own prayer and Bible passages are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: That resurrection does not forgive anyone’s sins, but sifts each person’s deserts. For it renders to each person according to his works.
translator_notes: Julian is explaining Romans 8:23–24. The last clause echoes Romans 2:6 (also Matthew 16:27; Psalm 62:12, LXX/Vulgate 61:13). ‘Sifts’ renders expurget: the contrast is between forgiving sin and assessing each person’s deserts. Augustine’s Matthew 12:32 and Luke 23:42 counterarguments are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: None of the righteous there will any longer bruise his body and bring it into subjection. No one will humble his soul with a hard bed and bodily filth.

No one will expose his blessed disregard for shame to insults, his cheeks to slaps, or his back to lashes. Nor will he strive to forge strength out of weakness. Frugality will not struggle with poverty, nor greatness of soul with grief, nor patience with pain.
translator_notes: Julian’s description of the blessed resurrection is interrupted by Augustine’s response; the separated portions are reunited. Bruising and subjecting the body recalls 1 Corinthians 9:27; cheeks and back offered to blows recall Isaiah 50:6; strength from weakness recalls Hebrews 11:34. The phrase felicem impudentiam is unusual: literally ‘blessed/happy shamelessness,’ apparently fearless disregard for the shame of insults. Augustine’s suggested addition about chastity is not Julian’s text.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Again you say ‘that no one hates his own flesh’ (Ephesians 5:29). Who denies it? Yet you assert that it must be broken down by the rigor of discipline.”

“So, when all sins are forgiven in baptism, that is, all the offspring of desire, if desire itself was also used up there, how do the saints fight against it, so that it may not conceive, ‘with bruising of the body, squalor of the limbs, breaking down of the flesh’? These are your words.”
translator_notes: ‘No one hates his own flesh’ is Julian’s use of Ephesians 5:29; the three phrases on bodily discipline are his words (compare 6.15.46). Augustine’s argument from James 1:14–15 and Romans 8:23 is his own and is not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Julian quotation and Scripture he cites
english: Do not be mistaken: neither the sexually immoral nor those who serve idols will possess God’s kingdom. (1 Corinthians 6:9–10)
And that is what you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified. (1 Corinthians 6:11)
If sexual desire were an evil, the person who is baptized would be free of it.
translator_notes: Augustine abbreviates the list in 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 with ‘and the rest’; the first paragraph translates only its surviving opening and conclusion, not the intervening unquoted items. His further biblical counterarguments are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “But if, as you indicated in one place, ‘the school of Dinomachus, which joins moral goodness and pleasure, pleases you’ … it is enough for us that you admit that one pleasure is unlawful and another lawful.”
translator_notes: Augustine refers to the earlier discussion at Against Julian 4.15.76. His polemical comparison with the monster Scylla and his claims about desire are not Julian’s language.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Now let us look at that most excellent sharpness of yours, by which you saw how to refute what I said: ‘that the desire of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not counted as sin; and although its guilt has already been loosed, it still remains.’ Against these words of mine you argue, most acute man, as though I had said that desire itself is freed from guilt through baptism, because I said ‘its guilt having already been loosed’: as though by ‘its’ I meant the guilt by which desire itself is guilty, so that, with that loosed, it remains acquitted.”

“But it suits you rather, since you proclaim it good, to say ‘that to its natural good,’ as you say of infants, ‘the good of sanctification is added,’ and let the desire of the flesh be a holy daughter of God.”
translator_notes: The words disputed in the first paragraph are Augustine’s own Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.25.28. In the second paragraph the words about the good of sanctification are what Julian and those who share his view say of infants; Augustine turns them, mockingly, toward desire.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: You have changed your position: forgetting your entire book, you have declared that lust is a substance.
translator_notes: Augustine preserves the accusation in indirect quotation and denies ever calling lust a substance. His discussion of other philosophers is his own explanation.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The third kind of quality is a passing state and an enduring quality of feeling. A passing state is placed among qualities because it is a starting point of qualities. To it are also assigned the experiences of mind or body that come and go in a moment. An enduring quality of feeling, however, arises from more powerful causes and clings to everyone in whom it occurs so firmly that it can be removed only with great efforts—or cannot be removed at all.
translator_notes: A technical distinction in the Aristotelian classification of qualities. ‘Passing state’ renders affectio; ‘enduring quality of feeling’ renders affectionalis qualitas. The latter concerns persistent dispositions, not simply emotions. Augustine’s explanatory examples and Romans 7 quotations are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Closing Aristotle’s wrestling school, let us return from it to the sacred Scriptures.
Sexual desire, then, is a sensation, and it is not an evil quality. Therefore, when sexual desire is diminished, sensation is diminished.
translator_notes: The introductory image is preserved as a quoted phrase embedded in Augustine’s report; the return to Scripture follows that report. Augustine’s objections and biblical counterarguments are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “So if you do not want to be contentious, I think you now see how rightly it is understood (though you try to explain it otherwise) that when the prophet had said, ‘Who is gracious to all your iniquities,’ which happens, of course, through the forgiveness of all sins, he at once added, ‘Who heals all your diseases’ (Psalm 103:3). By this he meant those evils with which the inner wars of the saints do not rest until they are healed, or, as far as they can be in this life, are lessened more and more.”
translator_notes: Julian’s own explanation of the verse is not given here; the reading of ‘diseases’ as the saints’ continuing inner struggle is Augustine’s.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “So ‘this wound, inflicted on the human race by the devil, compels whatever is born through it to be under the devil, as though he were rightfully picking fruit from his own shrub.’ You set out these words from my book to refute them, and you lie in wait for them as though I had said ‘that the devil is the author of human nature, and the maker of the very substance of which a human being consists.’”
translator_notes: Julian was challenging Augustine’s On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.23.26, on the devil’s wound and fruit from its own shrub. The allegation is disputed; Augustine’s tree-and-fruit explanation from Matthew 7:17 is his rebuttal.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [You] cannot imagine in what dialectical treatise I found that all opposites can be reversed.
In no dialectical treatise can it be found that all opposites can be reversed.
translator_notes: Julian challenges the logical reversal in Augustine’s claim that sins can pass in act but remain in guilt, while desire can remain in act but pass in guilt (On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.26.29). ‘Reversed’ renders reciprocationem, concerning whether the contrasted terms may exchange positions in the argument. Augustine quotes the objection twice with different wording; both forms are retained. His Luke 13:32 interpretation is excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Everything belonging to this class can be demonstrated by this one example. If someone has sacrificed to idols once, he can be burdened by the impiety of what he has done until he obtains forgiveness: the act has ended, but its guilt remains. But it is absolutely impossible for the act to remain and the guilt to depart—that is, for him to go on sacrificing to demons and yet be regarded as free from profanation.
translator_notes: Julian’s counterexample to Augustine’s claim that desire remains while its guilt is removed. Augustine accepts the account of idol sacrifice but rejects the proposed analogy.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: When the act has passed away, its guilt remains in the conscience of the person who sinned until it is forgiven.
translator_notes: Augustine’s subsequent account of where guilt remains, and his appeal to Colossians 2:14, are his own response.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The same pattern observed in the devil ought also to have been observed in an evil human being: no one should be condemned except for the faults of his own will. Therefore there is no original sin. Otherwise the work of him who created even the devil good cannot be approved.
translator_notes: Augustine preserves Julian’s argument in indirect quotation after citing his own On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.23.26. The argument concerns responsibility for one’s own voluntary faults.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: ‘Greater’ and ‘lesser’ belong to the defined category of quantity. But quantity is not only incapable of receiving contraries—which it has in common with quality and other categories—it also has no contrary, which it has in common with the definition of substance. Good and evil, however, are contraries.
translator_notes: A technical argument from Aristotelian categories against Augustine’s use of ‘lesser’ and ‘greater’ for humanity and angelic nature. The distinction between receiving contraries and having a contrary is preserved as the Latin states it; Augustine rejects its relevance.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If something properly ordered belongs to God, and something belonging to God is good, then being subject to the devil is good, since the order established by God is preserved in this way. It follows that rebelling against the devil is evil, since resistance disturbs the order established by God.
translator_notes: Julian argues against what he takes to follow from Augustine’s position. Augustine’s agricultural counterexample and scriptural citations are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The devil’s work is not allowed to pass through God’s work.
The root of evil cannot be placed in God’s gift.
The order of things does not allow evil to be produced from good, or anything unjust from what is just.
Sins are not born from something free from sin.
Guilt cannot be born from this work, which has no guilt.
translator_notes: A collection of Julian’s claims, repeated from Against Julian 1.8.41; 1.9.42–44; and 5.16.59,64. Augustine says Julian had also quoted Mani to compare with Augustine, but does not reproduce those Mani excerpts here.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: That man was cast into these miseries not by nature as a mother, but as by a stepmother.
No fuller’s cleansing herb cleanses me of the Manichean stain — as you say.
translator_notes: Julian’s taunt about Augustine’s former religion; the fuller’s cleansing herb recalls Malachi 3:2. Augustine’s preceding Cicero quotation and hypothetical Manichean argument are his own, not Julian excerpts.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “What I said in another book of mine, writing to Marcellinus, was ‘that the children of the woman who believed the serpent so as to be corrupted by lust are not set free except through the Son of the Virgin, who believed the angel so as to conceive without lust.’ You set it out in such a way, and wanted it taken in such a way, as though I had said ‘that the serpent had joined with Eve in bodily intercourse.’”
translator_notes: Julian quoted Augustine’s On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.28.56, contrasting Eve’s belief in the serpent with the Virgin’s belief in the angel. Augustine denies the sexual interpretation; his following 2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Corinthians 15:33 arguments are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Julian excerpts and reported appeal to authorities
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “So you have not, by your whole argument, crushed, as you boast, my assertion about the evil of fleshly desire and of original sin.”

“About the testimonies of the catholic writers Saint Basil of Caesarea and Saint John of Constantinople, whose meaning you said agrees with your views, I answered you in the first book of this work of mine with truth entirely sufficient and certain.”
“In the second book too we did enough to make it plain that it is not, as you abusively call it, ‘a conspiracy of lost men’ …”
“Hence also ‘the murmur of the people, which alone,’ you say, ‘is set against you by us,’ is not alone, since it rests on the authority of such great teachers …”
translator_notes: Augustine answers Julian’s claims here in his own voice; the first paragraph rejects Julian’s boast that he had demolished Augustine’s teaching. ‘A conspiracy of lost men’ and ‘the murmur of the people’ are Julian’s phrases (compare 1.7). The writings of Basil and John are discussed in Against Julian 1.5–6.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “As for the Apostle’s words where he says, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,’ and the rest up to where he says, ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from the body of this death?’ (Romans 7:18–24): you affirm ‘that I understand them otherwise than that whole passage ought to be understood.’ Without knowing it, you credit me with a great deal.”

“Against these movements, which must first be fought down so that they do not rule, and afterward healed so that they are wholly put out, you yourself also admitted that the saints wage glorious struggles.”
translator_notes: The Scripture gives the first and last words of the passage under dispute. ‘These movements’ are the movements of fleshly desire named in Augustine’s preceding sentence. The second paragraph refers back to Julian’s admission (Against Julian 3.21). Augustine’s account of how he changed his own reading, and the teachers he names, are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: It is contradictory for the person who says, ‘It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me,’ also to say, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.’ (Galatians 2:20; Romans 7:18)
You make the apostle say these things as though he meant that, despite his resistance, some hand of deadly pleasure dragged him off to prostitutes.
translator_notes: The second paragraph is Julian’s disputed characterization of Augustine’s interpretation, not an accusation that Paul actually visited prostitutes. Augustine’s Romans 7:20 response is excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “Why do you try in vain ‘to transfer these words to the pride of the Jews, as though the Apostle had represented in himself those who despised the gifts of Christ as not necessary for them’? For that is your conjecture. … But you say that they were despised by the Jews for this reason, ‘that he gave pardon for sins which they themselves had avoided through the admonition of the law.’”
translator_notes: Julian’s reading of Romans 7, in his words as Augustine reports them. Augustine rejects it; his description of Julian’s view of grace that follows is his own and is not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Julian quotations and Scripture he cites
english: The apostle emphasizes the power of habit.
Through the good law and the holy commandment, the minds of the wicked had become more savage, because no instruction could instill virtue without their own willing participation.

The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Has what is good, then, become death for me? Certainly not! But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment. (Romans 7:12–13)
translator_notes: Augustine expressly says Julian quoted Romans 7:12–13. The many surrounding Romans quotations are Augustine’s answer, not additional Julian citations in this section.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The expression ‘in whom all sinned’ is used as though it said ‘because of which all sinned,’ just as it says, ‘By what does a young man correct his way?’ (Romans 5:12; Psalm 119:9, LXX/Vulgate Psalm 118:9)

In this way, of course, all people are not to be understood as having sinned originally in one man, all together as though in the unity of one lump, but because that first man sinned; that is, when they imitate him, not when they are born from him.
translator_notes: The argument turns on the phrase translated ‘in whom’, which in Latin can also mean ‘in which’ or ‘by what’; Julian takes it in a causal sense. Both paragraphs are Julian’s words as Augustine quotes them; where the quotation ends is not marked clearly in the transcription, and the next sentence is taken as Augustine’s. Augustine’s examples of Cain and of a robber who kills are his answer and are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: By what does a young man correct his way? By guarding your words. (Psalm 119:9; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 118:9)
Moses fled at this word. (Acts 7:29)
translator_notes: Augustine explicitly identifies these as Julian’s supporting texts. They illustrate the proposed causal sense of ‘in/by’: ‘because of what’ or ‘because of this word.’ The psalm repeats the text discussed in 6.24.75. Augustine’s objections about imitation are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: But if he was speaking about the transmission of sin by descent, nowhere would it have been more appropriate for him to say, ‘Sin passed to all for this reason: because all were begotten through married people’s pleasure.’ He would have added, ‘It passes in this way: they flowed from the decaying flesh of the first man.’
translator_notes: Julian supplies wording he thinks Paul would have used if Romans 5:12 concerned inherited sin. These are Julian’s hypothetical formulations, not quotations of Scripture. Augustine’s competing hypothetical formulations are excluded.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “You do not want ‘many,’ which he said later, to be understood as ‘all,’ which he had said earlier, for you think that ‘many’ was said so that ‘all’ would not be understood.” (Romans 5:12,18–19)
translator_notes: The words ‘many’ and ‘all’ are from Romans 5. Augustine’s examples from Abraham and his other Bible passages are his answer and are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The proverb will no longer be used which says that parents ate sour grapes and their children’s teeth were set on edge. A son will not die for his father’s sin, nor a father for his son’s sin; the soul that sins will itself die. (Ezekiel 18:2–4,20)
translator_notes: Augustine identifies this as Julian’s final and supposedly strongest prophetic proof. The wording is Augustine’s summary of the passage Julian invokes, not an uninterrupted direct biblical quotation. Verse 20 is added because it supplies the father-and-son clause, beyond the source note’s Ezekiel 18:2–4. The subsequent biblical countertexts all belong to Augustine.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “That I have answered you on everything, Julian, and refuted everything by which, in four volumes, you thought and argued that original sin is not to be believed, and that the desire of the flesh cannot be blamed without condemning marriage, I think you see, if you are not obstinate.”

“… You dare, besides, to say that you have taken up war against the ungodly … You dare to join yourself to the company of the holy patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs and priests … You dare to say that you are being overcome by a fellowship of Manichaeans.”
translator_notes: Augustine’s summary of what Julian argued in four books, followed by claims of Julian’s that Augustine reports in order to answer them. The sayings Augustine puts in the mouths of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs and priests are his own answer and are not included.
